Special Commission of Inquiry
into Healthcare Funding
Before: The Commissioner,
Mr Richard Beasley SC
At Level 2, 121 Macquarie Street,
Sydney, New South Wales
Wednesday, 17 April 2024 at 10.00am
(Day 018)
Mr Ed Muston SC (Senior Counsel Assisting)
Mr Ross Glover (Counsel Assisting)
Dr Tamsin Waterhouse (Counsel Assisting)
Also present:
Mr Richard Cheney with Mr Hilbert Chiu for NSW Health

THE COMMISSIONER: Good morning.
MR MUSTON: Good morning. I think one issue that we can
deal with quickly at the outset, as I understand it, no
application is going to be made for any further restriction
on the publication of that passage of transcript that came
towards the end of the evidence of Mr Gregory, Lee Gregory,
yesterday. I don't think you need to do anything further
beyond noting that at 4.30, I think, this afternoon, in the
usual course, the transcript in its entirety will be
published.
THE COMMISSIONER: Yes. It would seem relatively
noncontroversial, what was non-commercial in confidence, or
whatever the concern was.
MR MUSTON: I should allow my learned friend to confirm
that my understanding is correct, but I think it is.
MR CHENEY: That's correct, Commissioner.
THE COMMISSIONER: Thanks.
MR MUSTON: We only have one witness today. It's Dr Ross
Kerridge, so I call him.
<ROSS KERRIDGE, sworn: [10.02am]
<EXAMINATION BY MR MUSTON:
MR MUSTON: Q. Could you state your full name for the
record, please?
A. Yes, Ross Kerridge.
Q. You are currently a senior staff specialist
anaesthetist at John Hunter Hospital and a conjoint
Associate Professor at the University of Newcastle?
A. Yes.
Q. Have you been provided with an outline of the evidence
that it is anticipated you will give?
A. Yes. The notes based on the discussion that we had
last week and on the original submission that I made.
Q. It is a document headed "Witness outline" at the top
with the name "Dr Ross Kerridge" in the first line?
A. Yes.

Q. Have you had an opportunity to read and consider that
document?
A. Yes.
Q. Does that document contain evidence which, to your
knowledge, is true and correct?
A. Yes.
MR MUSTON: In due course, I think the witness outline
will be included as part of the bulk tender, which
hopefully should speed things up a little bit this morning.
THE COMMISSIONER: Sure.
MR MUSTON: Q. You tell us in your outline that you
started out in your professional life as an anaesthetist?
A. I still am.
Q. Still an anaesthetist, but you pivoted in 1989 to what
you describe as the peri-operative system?
A. Yes. The first part of my comments was just to try
and say that I would like to think that I may be a little
bit different from many of my colleagues: I have
a reputation as being someone who comes up with new ideas
all the time.
Q. Can I ask you, how did that transition into the world
of peri-operative medicine happen --
A. Okay.
Q. -- back in 1989?
A. It's a long story, and it literally goes back 40 years
to about this month.
Q. Give us the abridged version.
A. Essentially, very early on in my training I realised
that there was potential for improving patient outcomes and
improving the efficiency of the system by changing the way
things were organised.
Q. In what sense?
A. With regard to patients having surgery, setting up
systems to optimise preparation beforehand to make that
more efficient.
Q. So what were the observations of the system at that

time that you made which led you to think that changes
might be useful?
A. At that time, the conventional model was that patients
would arrive for surgery one or two days before their
operation. That preparation would largely not start until
the patient actually arrived in hospital.
Q. When you talk about "preparation", what do you mean in
terms of preparation for procedures?
A. Assessment of the patient's medical status and
attempts to improve their medical status prior to surgery.
Q. So just to bring it to this point, in those days, it
was your observation that the assessment of the patient and
attempts to bring them to the point where they were ready
for their surgery would not start until very shortly before
the surgery was to occur?
A. Yes, and often our frustration as anaesthetists was
seeing the patient the afternoon or evening before surgery
and thinking "If only we had had a week, we could have
sorted this problem out", and we --
Q. What sort of problems?
A. Oh, investigations not being done; even things like
not knowing what medication the patient was taking.
Q. So what sort of things did you see at that time might
have been sorted out, to use your phrase, to produce better
outcomes?
A. Well, we set up a system whereby the routine became -
and I know it sounds ridiculously simple but it was a huge
battle at the time - to give the patient a questionnaire at
the time of booking in about their health, to identify any
health problems, to use that to go through at an
administrative level to triage the patients into those who
were straightforward and those where we needed to spend
some time gathering more information or improving their
health. Then, with that, we realised that there was no
reason why we couldn't bring patients into hospital on the
day of surgery and through a separate area to the surgical
wards, and that's all routine now, but I can tell you,
35 years ago I spilled a lot of blood and sweat and tears
convincing people to adapt that system, and it is estimated
that it saves the New South Wales health system about
250 million a year.
Q. You talk about the spilling of blood, sweat and tears

in order to get what you have described as relatively
simple changes. Why, at a systemic level, did you perceive
at that time that it was such a challenge to get those
changes made?
A. It's a conceptual leap. It's taking your colleagues
with you on a journey about changing the way they think
about the way to do things, having lots of thinking through
"If we bring someone in on the day, how can we be sure that
there will be a bed for them on the ward after their
surgery". I'm preparing a lecture for this which I'm going
to be giving in July, so it's very much in my head.
Q. So in terms of bringing the colleagues along, the
first bit of spilling of blood, sweat and tears was to
persuade your clinical colleagues --
A. Yes.
Q. -- that the system - that their systems needed to be
changed in order to review the patients earlier?
A. Yes, I remember at the time, the keys: you have to
have a vision, you have to share the vision and you have to
get your colleagues emotionally enthused with that vision.
When I say "colleagues", not just doctors - obviously they
were my first target - but also nurses, the surgeons, the
administrators, everybody involved, thinking about, "Yes,
we can do this".
Q. Can we break them up into their component parts. What
were the challenges that you faced in getting the doctors
and surgeons enthused at that time?
A. People have a varying range of acceptance of new
ideas. There is always a suspicion that "I'm going to lose
out on this", or "This is going to make my life more
difficult". One of the things I learned about surgeons is
that - it's a stereotype, I know, but in general, surgeons
are very much focused on wanting to do a job and wanting to
do surgery, and sometimes, people who are wanting to
improve the system demand that they come to meetings or
workshops or whatever, and really, they are happy to pass
on all that organisational task, as long as they are
confident that it will improve patient outcomes and will
make their work simpler and will guarantee the patient is
on the table having surgery, because that's what they like
doing.
Q. So how did you go about bringing those medical and
surgical colleagues along on the journey of change that was

the introduction of this peri-operative care --
A. Well, we had a few trial runs and trial examples, and
then going round and essentially selling the idea to people
as a concept.
Q. When you say "selling it", it was clinician by
clinician, is that the way the selling process happened?
A. Initially and, then, once we had the model working, we
would have workshops where I would bring one of my surgical
colleagues along to talk to the other surgeons at another
hospital or elsewhere.
Q. So that's the medical and surgical colleagues.
Nursing and allied health colleagues, were there any
challenges that you faced in bringing them along on the
journey?
A. Yes, again, this is sort of ancient history now but
still it's fun to recall it. One of the interesting things
was, I got a lot of push-back from some of the -
particularly the senior nurses, about the idea that the
patient wouldn't arrive on the ward until after their
surgery, and they are saying "No, they need to come into
hospital and settle into the hospital, meet the staff who
will be looking after them, have a good night's sleep
before surgery". You laugh. But we had huge fights about
this. But there are always one or two who were prepared to
give it a go and some who grudgingly came along.
Q. And what about management or the administration, what
challenges did you face in persuading administration of the
need for change?
A. That was a time when I really fell on my feet and
happened to be in the right place at the right time. It
was at Liverpool Hospital, and when I started there, only
a few weeks after I started there the minister announced
that they were going to make it a teaching hospital, and so
there was a sense of "There's going to be more money
arriving", and that empowered some of the people there, and
there was sort of a culture of willingness to accept new
ideas and I think a realisation that they needed to change
the way they were doing things because they were going to
be very short of beds, and so there was willingness to try
new ideas, and I was very lucky in that sense.
Q. That culture of a willingness to try new ideas, was
it, to your observation, simply born out of necessity or
was it something which involved the lucky or happy

coincidence of some people who were willing to embrace new
ideas within management positions?
A. A combination. There were some personalities, key
personalities, who got the idea and pushed it. Ian
Southwell, the deputy CEO, and the CEO of the health
service at the time were very supportive. Ken Hillman, the
head of anaesthetics there was very supportive, but there
was a culture in the hospital. But there was also, as you
say, a recognition that the resources were so stretched
that they had to try - had to be willing to change to try
new ways of doing things.
Q. In terms of the relationship between clinicians and
management, you have told us about having observed gulfs
between those two groups of people within the system. What
do you mean by that?
A. I trace it back to - in New South Wales, the
particular event goes back to the bitterness that arose
from the surgeons' dispute in the mid 1980s. I think that
set up a culture of antagonism between medical staff and
the senior administrators that may not have been there
before, or certainly became exacerbated, if it was, and
a culture of mistrust. I think that has continued to
evolve.
That said, while that's the case in New South Wales,
I think around the world, there has been that sort of thing
happen.
Thinking about it recently, I think there is the
culture of managerialism that has developed around the
world in all industries, which has arisen for various -
multiple reasons, but has been - underlying part of the
culture of managerialism is an assumption that your
workforce needs to be trained to be agile, flexible, and
that you should target your management strategy around
anticipating that you will want to unload staff. That's on
the basis that there will be plenty of staff turning up.
Q. So you refer to the culture of managerialism.
A. Yes.
Q. Can you explain in a little bit of detail exactly what
you mean?
A. My understanding of managerialism or some aspects of
managerialism is that it sees management as a discipline in
its own right and that you don't have to necessarily be

connected with your workforce, whether it be in a factory
or in a hospital or in any other industry.
Q. So that manifests itself in a number of ways. The
first you have just indicated is a view that shifts and
changes in workforce might need to be made quickly and on
an expectation that workforce will be available when needed
and able to be dispensed with when not needed. Are there
any other manifestations that you have in mind when you
refer to the culture of managerialism --
A. Well, I think - you know, I'm a doctor, I'm not
a management academic, but my understanding is that part of
that culture is that you shouldn't encourage identity and
culture and pride in the workforce and identifying with the
workforce as a team or as an institution, because that
makes it harder to be flexible and change things around,
whether you are managing a car manufacturing plant,
a service industry, a shopping industry - whatever sort of
industry.
But I think, contrasting to that, perhaps - and
certainly in hospitals - maybe we have inherited the ethos
from the military, and most of the leaders in health care
up until, I suppose, the mid '80s and even a bit later came
with the military culture where it was very much focused on
developing your younger troops and having a patriarchal
approach to developing the unit culture as a fighting unit,
so to speak, and that crossed over into the way hospitals
were managed.
In New South Wales, you had the giants of the New
South Wales health system like Roger Vanderfield at North
Shore and Bernie Amos at Westmead, Bill Monaghan at
St George. These were people who were respected and
regarded fondly and people who had been there in the
trenches and had gone up the system and had a sense of that
they would nurture the medical students, the residents, the
registrars, and they would nurture loyalty of them back to
the hospital. Obviously this is on the medical side, but
you had the similar sort of things going on in nursing as
well.
Q. So the first of the things that you attribute to or
characterise as creating the gulfs is the rise of
managerialism. Are there other things that you feel
contribute to the creation of a gulf between management and
clinicians?

A. The behaviour of some clinicians has certainly not
helped.
Q. In what way?
A. Oh, there is no doubt there have been clinicians who
have exploited the system and not put in. But in the
overall scheme of things, I think that's more of an
emotional issue rather than a real issue. But certainly
there are some who, you know, don't help the cause, don't
help trust.
But that said, the vast majority of doctors, I think
those working in the public system are motivated by some
degree of, you know, loyalty; they want to do something;
they want to feel that they are doing a good job. But, you
know, that requires a sense of doing meaningful work, of
being able to do it well, meaningful and mastery, and
a sense of having some control over your work, some
autonomy, which would presume that that's not doing
whatever you want, but in a system sense, would be that
your opinion and your thoughts about how to make the system
better would be listened to and would be respected.
Q. We've talked a little bit about some of the history.
Is it your perception that the gulfs that you speak of
are still present as between management and clinicians, at
least within your LHD?
A. I have put it in my written submission and I won't
resile from it, that I think what I've seen in Hunter New
England LHD has been quite interesting, that 15, 20 years
ago we were performing at a very high level. There was
a real sense that we were doing things well, and at one
stage, we were winning so many of the premier's annual
awards that it was getting a bit embarrassing. And in the
last 15 years, I think we've gone through a cycle we're the
executive leadership has been perhaps too focused on
financial outcomes and has, even openly, made comments,
negative comments, particularly about the medical staff
being unhelpful, about "they are impossible to work with",
and so on, and that has led to a loss of performance, you
know, we're not doing as well. We talk to colleagues in
other parts of the state and we hear different messages
about the way they are going.
Q. Can I just ask you about the two issues you have
raised. The first is an excessive focus, or what you
perceive to be an excessive focus on financial performance.

A. Yes.
Q. How does that manifest itself in terms of what you
observe in doing your day-to-day work?
A. Yes, one of the frustrating things is - you know,
I don't think anyone labours under the illusion that there
is infinite resources, but what - I've picked up the term
for somewhere, dysfunctional parsimony, of things where,
because of financial restraints, a culture of not doing
something that may risk going over budget or may risk an
unexpected expense is not done, even if it has potential
for saving the system a lot of money. My list of examples
of that is so long that --
Q. Could you give us one?
A. -- we would be here all day.
Q. Pick a good one?
A. A classic one is the delay in getting the patient to
the operating theatre for surgery that has to be done
before the patient can be discharged. Our delay in getting
fractured necks of femur to operating theatres, we've
tracked it going up in the last two to three years. You
know, we're a very busy hospital but I think - sorry,
I can't remember the numbers but I have the graph that
I could supply you, but our time to get a patient for
a fractured neck of femur to operating theatres to get it
fixed is tracking up to 48 hours, and the length of stay
has increased at the same time. I think the reason you
can't get to operating theatres is because we're not
staffing enough operating theatres, and so, therefore,
we're continually running out of time. But that's not
saving any money.
We recently had a registrar of - our own registrar,
was in hospital with a condition that required surgery, and
in fact, his surgery was put off and put off for three days
and was finally done because someone realised that he was
actually rostered on for new year's eve and if he wasn't
back at work by then, they wouldn't be able to fill that
slot. So they said "Look, we've got to get him done." But
I thought he wasn't going anywhere until the surgery was
done. They are silly examples, but --
Q. But looking at that example you give about a delay to
surgery, as I understand it, the delay to surgery has
consequences which are financial for the LHD?

A. Yes. It results in a net increase in cost.
Q. But is it an obsessive focus on finance which has led
to or which is standing in the way of those changes being
made? It would seem that, from a financial point of view,
even if you did focus obsessively on finance, that change
should have been made.
A. I think one manifestation of this is, if you say,
"We're going to be very careful about the number of nurses
that we roster on for the post anaesthetic care unit, or
recovery" - the area you go to after, from the operating
theatre, so that there is, you know, very little slack in
the system.
Then, if there is - for some reason you get an excess
number of nurses call in sick, then they say "Oh, we can't
move the patients out". Recovery is in bed block, code
red. And so we have to hold the patient in the operating
theatre and recover them in the operating theatre rather
than get them out to recovery and get the operating theatre
cleaned up and the next case under way. You think if you
had had enough staff, including some extra staff for sick
leave, even though that may require some extra budget there
or some flexibility, then we could have used that time in
the operating theatres. An operating theatre, whether you
use it or not, once staffed, it costs about $2,000 an hour.
Q. So from the point of view, as best you are aware,
where is the - at what level is this focus on financial
matters causing problems? Is it causing a problem at the
LHD level in the sense that there is someone at the top of
the LHD that is making decisions based on finances which
are having the consequences that you allude to, or is it
decisions are made at the LHD level which result in finance
or a budget being given to various parts of the
organisation, and is it the decisions being made at those
lower levels within the organisation about the way in which
they might use their budget which is the cause of the
problem, or possibly all of the above?
A. Look, I think all of the above and none of the above,
and, I mean - sorry, with respect, even the tone of your
question is "Who is making this stupid decision?" And
I don't think that's the problem. It's not anyone making
a bad decision themselves, but they are in a set of
circumstances where the structure, the financial
decision-making, the accountability, the culture of, the
dangers of going over budget versus the dangers of not

being as productive as you could be all conspire to drive
people to make a decision that avoids taking a risk that
may improve the system. Everyone's trying to do the right
thing, but they face a complex set of forces when they are
making their decisions.
Q. You say it is all of the above and none of the above.
Is there, insofar as you are aware, anyone within the
system in your LHD who is taking a global view of all of
these little decisions and reaching a view about whether or
not it's the best way to be doing things? You may not
know, but --
A. Look, I have referred to the fortunes of our
particular LHD, and again, I have put it in writing and
I definitely agree with it. We have had a change in our
executive leadership just recently and I think the
underlying morale in our LHD has improved as a result, I've
great confidence that we are heading in the right
direction, but it is going to take a long, long time.
Q. So is the lack of morale or the reduction in morale
attributable to the gulfs that you speak of in your
outline?
A. I think the sense of not being valued, even things
like, when was it, about 10 years ago, we had all the milk
taken out of the fridges because, you know, there was - it
got on the front page of the Newcastle Herald, actually -
because the general manager found out that some people had
been daring to eat breakfast at work and so all the milk
was taken out of the fridges and only enough milk to make
a milk coffee was available. But, look, we've recently had
the service manager in surgery said, "Look, bring in milk
and biscuits. Yes, it will cost us a little bit, but if it
makes people happier, that's worthwhile. That's a great
investment". Unfortunately, she's been snaffled by the
private sector since.
MR CHENEY: I don't wish to be popping up all the time --
THE COMMISSIONER: You've only popped up once so far.
MR CHENEY: -- but I'm conscious of the constraints on you
under section 9 of the Act about only receiving evidence
that would be likely to be admissible in civil proceedings.
I don't mean this in any way to diminish Dr Kerridge's view
of things and I know he is here to assist the Inquiry, but
there are some limits to the sort of --

THE COMMISSIONER: Sorry, I can't hear you.
MR CHENEY: There are some limits to the sort of anecdotal
material that you should be asked to receive, and in my
submission, the witness should be asked to --
THE COMMISSIONER: The issue of the milk can't embarrass -
is that an issue for NSW Health?
MR CHENEY: I'm not suggesting it is, Commissioner, but it
does point to the nature of this evidence as being so
generalist and wide-ranging without any necessary specifics
that bear on your terms of reference. It's like grasping
smoke, for those of us who have to deal with it.
THE COMMISSIONER: Give me an example that is particularly
difficult for you, of evidence given by the witness so far
that is causing you difficulty and concern?
MR CHENEY: For example, there are multiple references to
this witness's perception of what clinicians' view is of
the relationship between them and management, and in no
world would that sort of evidence in that form be
admissible in any civil proceeding. This witness is
purporting to give evidence of what the perception is of
other clinicians about management. Now --
THE COMMISSIONER: Look, we will proceed, and I will
direct my attention in a more focused way on the issues
that you have just raised, having not appreciated that
there was any concern on your behalf. Now I do, so I will
focus more closely on issues of admissibility to the extent
that I need to, and we will see how we go from now on.
MR CHENEY: Commissioner, we appreciate it is difficult
for counsel assisting and for the witness, and there has to
be some flexibility in this, but it's just that we think
there should be an attempt to confine the witness to
matters bearing on the terms of reference.
THE COMMISSIONER: I'm sure Mr Muston has heard everything
you have just said.
MR CHENEY: Thank you, Commissioner.
MR MUSTON: Q. So, in terms of the creation of gulfs, it

is your perception that issues around staff morale feature
prominently in them. Is there anything that you think
could be changed about the system which would close some of
these gulfs, from the perspective of a clinician working
within that system?
A. Again, I'm trying to - one of the things that
I mentioned in my initial submission that I thought was
particularly striking - and, again, this is now 20 years
ago - we had a program with some external consultants
looking at our clinical processes and clinical process
redesign, and a big part of that was what were called
tag-alongs, and these were done as a sort of physical thing
of designating someone to actually walk through, following
a person at work or following somewhere, and just seeing
what actually happened. One of them was following
a specimen of blood from emergency until the result was
obtained in emergency, and looking at all the delays that
happened and tracking exactly what actually happened.
One that I did was following along one of the
emergency medicine specialists, with a clipboard, and just
tracking exactly what they did.
Another, we got a senior neurosurgeon at the time who
was just on the cusp of retiring to sit at the front desk
of the operating theatres for three hours and watch what
happened, and the feedback afterwards, he was absolutely
flabbergasted. He said "I've been working here for 30
years. I had never realised just how chaotic it was".
Q. Is your point around that that if those who are
involved in the management of the LHD were in a physical
sense more invited to or sought to obtain a better sense of
what a day in the life of a clinician looks like, that that
would be one way of working towards closing some of these
gulfs?
A. Yes. In that particular case, with the surgeon at the
front desk, he realised part of the problem was the younger
surgeons coming up to book cases not knowing who to talk
to. He came up with the idea of putting a red hat on the
nurse in charge of the operating theatres for the day.
A very simple thing, but it improved things dramatically.
There are lots of things like that.
Q. You tell us in paragraph 5 of your statement about
some genuine and successful attempts to engage management
and clinicians. You refer to two particular programs, the

Greater Metropolitan Transition Task Force and the Maggi
program?
A. Yes.
Q. Can you just describe what the greater metropolitan
transition task force was?
A. Well, that was in the early 2000s, formed under Kerry
Goulston, with, if you like, ministerial imprimatur to form
structures for clinicians to form working groups to work
together and confront some of the challenges about service
delivery particularly across Sydney, and things like, you
know, should every hospital be doing every type of service,
and so on.
Q. So that was a service planning task force?
A. Service planning and service redesign, yes.
Q. And is the point that you seek to make there in
paragraph 5 that, in undertaking that planning and redesign
process, there was an engagement of both management and
clinicians in a collaborative way to work out the solution?
A. Yes, and I think those saying - part of the deal was
that the department, I think it was the department then,
were saying that "We are prepared to invest more money in
this particular service, but you need to decide where the
service is going to be delivered, where the big new fancy
equipment is going to go, and it's not going to go in every
hospital and you have to have some rationale for doing it
and it has to be your decisions".
Q. From the perspective of a clinician, how do you think
the system could deal with the making of those decisions
where, for example, giving, to use your term, the big fancy
new piece of machinery to one hospital and not another will
inevitably mean there is a group of clinicians at that
other hospital who don't get something they'd quite like?
A. Yes.
Q. How does the system deal with that?
A. I think having structures such as that, that actually
does engage them in making the decisions.
Q. When you say "engage them", these are enabling them to
participate in the process, but is there something more
than that, in terms of the engagement? Is it the fact that
these decisions appear to have a strategic objective, that
they are brought into and able to understand, which is part

of that process, or is there more?
A. I think that sense of being empowered and being
listened to.
Q. What about the Maggi program in Hunter New England --
A. That's the program I was referring to.
Q. So the greater metropolitan task force and the Maggi
program are one and the same thing?
A. No, sorry, the Maggi program was the program I was
talking to where we were doing tag-alongs and other things
and getting people to solve their own problems.
Q. You then tell us that some recommendations were
implemented following the Garling Commission. What were
the particular recommendations that you have in mind,
without needing to give us details? Were there any
particular changes post Garling, just leading up to
a question about the ways in which you feel they have
become de-energised, to use your language?
A. I think there are 130-something recommendations from
Garling.
Q. When you tell us, though, that some of the changes
have been de-energised, first question: what were the
particular changes that you had in mind?
A. One of the big themes in Garling's report was the
great schism. From memory he came up with some comparison
to some event in the early days of the church I think and
the need to --
Q. That sounds about right.
A. And the need to - I think that set the tone for taking
this seriously, and it certainly, I think, was listened to
for a while, and I'm not saying that that has gone
completely, although I think, as I touched on before, in
our particular area, you know, we went from being, you
know, up here to down there and we're now on the way back

re-emphasised.
Q. So do we gather what you are saying in paragraph 6 is

your perception, an increased focus on attempting to
engage - develop engagement between management and
clinicians?
A. Yes, and the CEC and the ACI.

Q. The CEC and the ACI were part of that process?
A. Yes, yes.
Q. But in terms of a general enthusiasm for engagement,
you feel it's drifted off?
A. Yes.
Q. But are there any particular examples that you are
able to give or particular instances that you point to
which you say reflect the disengagement or de-energising?
You may not be able to.
A. No.
Q. You tell us about the medical staff councils in your

A. I think they are part of the solution, yes.
Q. At least - you are a member of a medical staff council

A. Sorry?
Q. Are you a member of a medical staff council within
your hospital?
A. Yes, we have a medical staff council, yes.
Q. And you are a participant in that process?
A. Yes.
Q. As a clinician in that hospital?
A. Yes.
Q. Do you feel that it is actually being effectively

A. It is having more - we're being listened to more now.
Q. What do you see as being the positives about the way

A. We have a group of - and the medical staff council was

THE COMMISSIONER: Can I just - sorry, can I interrupt?

My feeling is - and it is not just my feeling, other

little bit too top-down.
Q. What do you mean by that?
A. The ACI is coming up with this to be implemented,
rather than encouraging ideas from the floor.
Q. Is that something you have - are you part of the - do
you play a role in the peri-operative network?
A. I'm on the anaesthesia peri-operative network.
Q. Is the issue you have just raised about perhaps not
encouraging ideas going up towards the ACI rather than
something being dictated from on high - is that something
you have raised? Forgive the way I have expressed that,
you might want to put it in different words, but is that
something that has been raised in your particular clinical

A. No, look, I haven't raised it as such, but having gone

Q. Perhaps if I can put it this way: tell me if this is
or isn't your opinion or you have some nuance about it, but
in terms of the Agency for Clinical Innovation, and its
clinical networks like peri-operative medicine, the network
relating to improvements in elective surgery, that sort of
thing, I take it you still view those networks as having
value?
A. Absolutely. Yes.
Q. But from time to time, I suppose like any networks,
sometimes they operate better than at other times?
A. Yes.
Q. And that might depend on who is on the actual network?
A. Yes. I think the --
Q. Is there anything further you wanted to add to that?
Because obviously I put a very broad proposition to you.
If you feel that there is some nuance or something
additional, please go ahead.
A. Look, I do think the agency - the ACI is a good thing.
It has been doing some good things. But I think still
seeing that part of its culture is to generate a sense of
potential for innovation and creativity and problem solving
at the local level, and that if people come up with good
ideas, then they can be fed up the chain and spread and
they will get recognition for that.
Q. So that's like more of a tweak you would like to see

A. Yes.

THE COMMISSIONER: Thank you.
MR MUSTON: Q. I think we were --
THE COMMISSIONER: Sorry, I distracted you from medical
staff --
MR MUSTON: Q. Medical staff councils. You had told us
prior to or as at about 2017, the medical staff council
that you were involved in had gone into abeyance or,
rather, largely gone into abeyance?
A. It had been in abeyance for a while and a group of us
felt that --
Q. Can I - when you say "abeyance", what do you mean by
that? Were there not meetings being held or --
A. We weren't having regular meetings and --
Q. And you personally weren't attending meetings,
obviously, if they weren't happening?
A. We weren't having them and there was a sense that in
terms of engaging with the executive, that there wasn't
much point anyway.
Q. And when you say that, from your point of view, what
was it that led you to feel that participating in or
initiating regular meetings with the medical staff council
at that time was not something that would be worth doing,
from your personal perspective?
A. Well, it wasn't there.
Q. Did you seek to revitalise it at some point?
A. Yes.
Q. What was it that led you --
A. Not me - me with some others.
Q. Just speaking from your personal experience, what was
it that led you to think a revitalisation of the medical
staff council would be a good thing to do at that
particular moment in time?
A. I think there was a group of us who were frustrated
that there wasn't a good esprit de corps in our hospital,
that we could do better, some who were wanting that,
perhaps romantically, but - and recognising that there is,
in the Health Services Act, it does exist, and so that we
should - you know, it is up to us to make it exist.

Q. So you saw the opportunity for the revitalisation of
the medical staff council to bring a bit of camaraderie and
esprit de corps to the workforce?
A. Yes.
Q. In terms of the reasons for it having drifted away or
gone into abeyance, is it just that everyone was very busy,
or was there some other reason, at least insofar as you saw
it, based on your perception, for the medical staff council
having, prior to its revitalisation, ceased to --
A. We didn't have any administrative support, and so if

reminders to people and doing administrative tasks. If you
don't have some support for doing that, or if, as was the
case, the hospital refusing to give us a list of all the
medical staff and their emails, it makes it pretty
difficult to send out your emails when you don't know who
the staff are.
Q. At the time of or since the revitalisation has some
administrative support been provided?
A. Yes.
Q. Has that been effective in re-energising, to use your
term, the medical staff council?
A. It's a work in process, but we've had - you know,
we're having an autumn dinner in May and having another
event later in the year. We're having meetings of the
executive once a month, the CEO attends by Zoom for a short
while, and we've got the current head of the medical staff
council who is exceptionally energetic and well organised
and is doing a good job, I think.
Q. So the medical staff council provides an opportunity
to facilitate dinners and social functions which build that
camaraderie and esprit de corps?
A. Yes, look, that's a soft thing but I think also you
would hope, even though John Hunter is a big hospital, that
providing some avenue for communication up the chain if
there is a department that is getting into strife,
sometimes you get - a group of a clinical department will
start getting unhappy with each other and that --
Q. You have anticipated my next question. To what extent
do you think the revitalised medical staff council at your
hospital has improved the engagement between clinicians and

management?
A. Well, as I say, the current CEO has made a point of
coming along and talking about what's going on, and I think
that's been a welcome development.
Q. So is it your view that a CEO who is interested in
engaging with and collaborating with the medical staff
council, combined with a chair of the medical staff council
who is energetic, I think was the term you used --
A. Yes.
Q. -- is what's really produced that greater level of
engagement?
A. And we have some protected administrative time, an
admin officer, and there is an understanding that part of
that person's role is to send out all the notices and so on
and so forth.
Q. And has that, to your observation, helped to bridge
some of the gulfs, at least in your hospital, between
management and clinicians in a way that has been positive?
A. It is a work in progress.
Q. Is it upward progress, though?
A. Yes, yes.
Q. You have given us in your outline some broad examples
of innovation. We've talked about peri-operative care and
you have discussed in paragraphs 17 and 18 at a very high
level the potential benefits of expending it to
postoperative care. In paragraph 19 you refer to other
clinician-led innovations and refer to particular
innovations which presumably you have some particular
things in mind. Do you have paragraph - sorry, I might be
jumping ahead of you. Do you have paragraph 19 handy?
A. Well --
Q. You refer to opportunities for system improvement and
waste avoidance?
A. In surgery at the moment, we are trialling getting
geriatricians involved in looking after surgical patients
in - acute post-surgical patients, or pre-surgical
patients, for that matter. You know, many of our patients
are elderly and frail. It's not necessarily in the skill
set of the surgeons to do that at the high level that the
geriatricians can do, and yet that has traditionally been
the model.

We have trialled having geriatricians assigned to that
unit. We've got some preliminary data showing that this
led to an improvement in outcomes and a reduction in length
of stay, and there is experience at other hospitals with
this.
Q. Is that an example of an opportunity for system
improvement and waste avoidance that has been successfully
implemented, or in the process of being successfully
implemented?
A. Well, so far, yes, yes. Now, that would require extra
commitment of funds, and, yes, we get that that's
a problem, but --
Q. Just in relation to that, are you involved in
discussions with anyone around the potential for additional
funds being provided for that project?
A. I'm not directly involved, but those discussions are
going on. But that's an example.
A better example is a trial that we're doing at the
moment. You would be aware of the things that you put on
the legs that squeeze your legs after major surgery and
that you have to have on if you have had major surgery and
prevent clots in your legs.
Q. I am now.
A. One of our surgeons who has a particular penchant for
challenging myths has organised a trial looking at what the
evidence for that is, and in fact, the evidence isn't
nearly as good as you would like to think.
Q. So is that an example that you give of an opportunity
for system improvement where, subject to the findings of
that study, there may be potential for a change or an
adjustment to the system which could produce some savings?
A. Yes. In fact, the cost of those devices, you know,
obviously in the trial, half the patients are not going to
have those devices put on, and the cost of those devices is
enough to fund the trial, like the cost of not using them
is enough to fund the trial.
Q. You refer in your outline to some opportunities for
system improvement and waste avoidance which have been
identified but then become the source of frustration,
disappointment and burnout for the clinicians, who feel

they are being ignored by management.
A. Yes.
Q. Can I ask you this question first: have you
personally identified any opportunity for system
improvement which falls into that category - that is to
say, have you personally felt frustrated, disappointed or
burnt out by being ignored --
A. Me personally, so many times. I will give you one
example.
Q. A personal example, if possible.
A. And I checked in with - well, she's now a staff
specialist. We have looked at the question of whether we
need to do what we call a group and screen blood test on
what level of patients prior to major surgery.
Q. When you say "we", this is something that you have
been involved in?
A. Yes, I'm the - I'm one of the co-authors of the trial.
Q. Okay. Sorry, I interrupted you.
A. But we've looked at - we have very good data about
cross-matching of blood transfusion in Hunter New England
for reasons that go back to the time when the blood
transfusions service started in 1947. The data is complex
to analyse, but nevertheless is there, and we looked at
that in a simple analysis, and the results of that analysis
appeared to suggest that we could avoid doing that group
and screen test, which costs the system about $60/$70 per
time, I think. We could avoid that on certainly
three-quarters of the patients that we're currently doing
them on. But we need the evidence to back that.
That requires the data to be analysed. We presented
the initial report, or when I say "we", my colleague, who
at the time was a registrar, and is now a staff specialist,
presented that at the College of Anaesthetists meeting in
2019 and got the prize for the best presentation.
Embarrassingly, we found that some of the data we needed to
reanalyse, we're still - we've been putting in "Hey, we
need this data analysed, and that needs help from IT and
from clinical information to get that data analysed", but
we can't get an imprimatur to say "Look, get that done".
We keep on being - "Oh, we're getting around to it".
Q. When you say you can't get an imprimatur, who have you

approached in an attempt to get that analysis work done?
A. Well, this crosses between the LHD and the blood
service. So, you know, we need to sit down, and we've
offered to fund it out of some research trust funds that
we've got, but we don't have engagement. It's not going to
save them any money, in fact, it's going to lose business
for them because we won't be sending blood samples to
pathology.
Q. When you say "them", who is the "them" who you are not
getting engagement from?
A. Pathology and the blood service.
THE COMMISSIONER: Q. Doctor, is what you are addressing
now related to that the ACI, in its peri-operative network,
has a peri-operative tool kit, which has a section on blood
watch, which I think deals with transfusions.
A. Yes.
Q. Is that the area you are talking about now?
A. Yes. Yes. There is a general move to - one, we want
to reduce the amount that we're transfusing patients,
because we've realised that often it's of no benefit to the
patient; but that has led on to further ramifications
about, given how much better the surgeons are now at not
spilling blood, do we really need to be as prepared for
a massive blood loss as we traditionally have been. But in
order to prove the safety of that, you have to analyse the
data, and we have some unique data in Newcastle, not just
about the incidence of transfusion but the timing of
transfusion. But I actually checked in with my colleague
yesterday and she was saying, "Oh, yes, look, I followed up
with Monique and she said" - you know, but you can see that
she's just getting so frustrated. It's there, and a young
specialist like her, with a bit of a bent for research, we
should be saying, "Look, let's fast-track this. Let's get
it done. Let's sort it out. Let's get it published. This
is fantastic". Instead, she's getting frustrated and burnt
out and saying, "Why do you bother".
Q. Can I also ask you a question so that I understand
more fully what you have said in paragraph 12 of the
outline, where we're talking about advancements in
peri-operative care and earlier medical assessments. An
earlier medical assessment, how should I understand that,
in terms of how much earlier than the surgery?
A. Okay. The reality in our hospital and our waiting

time, particularly for joint replacements, is long.
Q. Yes.
A. Your ideal would be to say - well, in fact our ideal
would be, rather than even put people on the waiting list,
say, "No, we don't accept the booking until we've gone
through and decided." We want to assess the patient from
a comprehensive medical state, identify any issues and then
say, "Yes, we agree with the orthopaedic surgeon that this
is the way to go" or sometimes, you know, the orthopod may
have, on the day, said, "We will book you in", but --
Q. Ideally, how long is this before an actual surgery
date?
A. Well, that should happen even before they go on the
waiting list.
Q. So a long time?
A. We should identify, are there any issues, say, their
cardiac state, their diabetes; should we divert them,
divert the patient into a physiotherapy and weight loss
program, rather than a knee replacement?
Q. And this happens at John Hunter and your LHD?
A. No, it doesn't. We would like to do that, but --
Q. Why doesn't it happen?
A. It's all too hard.
Q. I haven't looked at, in detail, so I'm asking
a question from a lack of knowledge, but I know that, for
example, I've just mentioned the peri-operative tool kit in
the Agency for Clinical Innovation, and I think there is
a range of questionnaires now about people's health before
they have elective surgery.
A. Yes.
Q. Do you know of any LHDs that are, for example, for
things like elective surgery joint replacements that are
engaging in this process of seeing patients well before the
surgery date?
A. I think North Shore is, or they have done it. I'm not
sure if they are --
Q. They've told us they have, certainly. But it's not
routine, to your knowledge, at least, across other LHDs or
other hospitals?

A. No, and I mean, we see them a month beforehand, which
is still, like, compared to what it was 20 years ago, is
fantastic, but --
Q. But if surgery could be avoided, for example, by
weight loss or some other behavioural change, a month is
inadequate; correct?
A. Yes. Or, you know, maybe we need to make the
difficult decision to say, "No, sorry, in your case, a knee
replacement isn't appropriate."
Q. For whatever medical reason.
A. For whatever reason. But the surgeons, you know,
particularly if they have been put on the list by
a surgical trainee, you know, they are people with
a hammer - sorry.
Q. Yes, understood.
A. You know, if the only tool you have got is a hammer,
then every problem looks like a nail. That's one of the
ironies, that to put someone on the waiting list is easy.
To talk them out of and convince the patient and hopefully
have them not, you know, raising merry hell as to why we
shouldn't go ahead with surgery - whether it be a knee
replacement or sometimes complex - say bowel cancer surgery
in a very frail patient - it may require a difficult
conversation with the patient and their family as to why,
in this case, you are better not to go ahead with surgery,
accept that the cancer is there, and, given that your life
expectancy is, say, 12 months, whatever, that you are
better not to take the risk of surgery. I've done that,
but it takes a long time.
MR MUSTON: Q. And the earlier those conversations
happen in the pathway, the better, presumably?
A. The earlier the better, yes, trying to - if you have
got someone who, you know - and the surgeons themselves
would like this, the ability to say "Look" - and sometimes
they - you know, we do it as a favour, say "Look, before we
actually even book you for surgery, I want you to talk to
the anaesthetist". We may all have the same feeling, but
having that early assessment with a multidisciplinary team,
and hopefully getting the patient and the family to
understand that the surgeon's a perfectly competent
surgeon, you know, there is nothing wrong with that, but
given that patient's physiological state, and so on, it's
not appropriate to go ahead with surgery.

THE COMMISSIONER: Q. To a layperson - and I am
a layperson - it seems like what you are describing and
others have described to us, the Inquiry team, about early
assessments for people on elective surgery lists - and I'm
assuming this doesn't happen, and maybe it does happen and
I will end up being told - it seems like such an obvious
thing that can lead to better health outcomes --
A. Yes.
Q. -- and lack of waste, that it's hard to understand why
these early assessments wouldn't always happen across all
of our public hospitals and LHDs. Do you understand why
it's not routine?
A. It's a change. It's a change in process. In my time,
there's been one executive person who's actually come down
to our pre-op clinic and sat in and seen what we do. And
I checked with the nurse manager last week about that.
She's now been in her position now for about seven years.

Q. Has any qualified person - I use "qualified person" in
a broad sense, it might include surgeons, anaesthetists,
even people in allied health - has anyone with expertise
and experience ever said to you "There is no need for early
assessments of people that are on elective surgery waiting
lists" - for example, for joint replacements - "We can just
see them a week before or a few weeks before the surgery
and go ahead, there is no need to see them 12 months
before"?
A. No, not - no, I don't think so.
Q. That doesn't surprise me, but - yes.
A. Yes, not the way we're doing things now, yes.
THE COMMISSIONER: Sorry, I interrupted you, and I've
forgotten what you were asking when I interrupted you, but
I assume you will remember.
MR MUSTON: You have provoked me to ask another question,
anyway.
Q. To the extent that you are of the view that earlier

assessment - well, let me take it in two parts. You have
expressed the view that seeing patients a month before
their surgery is a great improvement on the old days?
A. Yes.
Q. I gather it's your view that if you could see them
earlier - and that is, before they are put on the list for
elective surgery - that would be the best practice, or
optimum?
A. Yes, not necessarily seeing them. You know, most
patients - yes, most patients, we don't need to see, even
in a complex hospital like ours, you know, we're dealing
with complex patients and often socioeconomically and
medically challenged. But we certainly don't need to see
all of them. But they need to be - we need information
about them gathered at the time that they are booked, and
look at that and triage at the time, and ideally, then, the
ones that are high risk, you would see them then rather
than wait until shortly before surgery.
Q. And that feeds in to what you tell us in your outline
about the importance of collaboration with primary health
care providers and, in particular, general practitioners?
A. Yes. I'm a great believer in general practice and
I think for as much as hospitals are problems, fixing up
the general practice system in Australia would be the
biggest thing we could do for health care but I know that's
outside --
THE COMMISSIONER: Q. Should I understand your last
answer to mean that provided you've got the data and
medical history about a patient on an elective surgery
list, and you might see someone that has some form of, say,
hereditary hip degeneration, they are 50 years of age, they
are within a good weight band, and they don't have any
comorbidities, they are not necessarily the sort of person
you need to see, but if someone is either elderly or they
are obviously in an obese category --
A. Yes.
Q. -- or they have some other comorbidities, they are the
people that need assessment as to whether surgery is
appropriate?
A. Yes.
MR MUSTON: Q. That would have the added benefit, would
it, potentially, of meaning the first category of patient,

the person in their 50s, who is fit, healthy, good weight
but just quite disabled by a hip problem, might actually be
able to be seen sooner and treated and sent back to have
a fulfilling life with --
A. Yes, I'm wondering, am I picking up that this happened
to you or?
THE COMMISSIONER: Q. No, I have shared my medical
history with the entire team. I won't go into detail now,
but it could generally be described as good. But all the
joints I've got are still the ones I was born with.
A. You will laugh at this story --
MR MUSTON: Q. Before the story, can I just ask, is that
right that if you did have this information sharing and the
triaging as you describe it at that very early stage, would
that enable a more nuanced allocation within the waiting
list?
A. Yes.
Q. So that those people who don't actually need to do
anything but really do need to get the surgery to get on
with their lives can be treated potentially sooner?
A. Yes. (Nods)
Q. While those who should be - you are nodding, so I take
that as a "yes" - should potentially spend some time
pre-habilitating --
A. We had a patient last year who, unbeknownst to the
surgeon, had been admitted to another hospital with
disabling hip pain and could not be discharged, and came
along to our clinic from that hospital for her pre-op
assessment for surgery in a month's time. "What's going on
here? Like, you are already in hospital." She can't be
discharged, because she lived alone, and in that case, we

Q. In order to bring about a change of the type you
suggest might be worth making, namely, that earlier
assessment, initially on the data, then in relevant cases
through seeing the patient before they get on to the list,
what would need to happen? How would that change get made?
What would you do, let's take it from your perspective, to
bring about that change?
A. I think our managers - you know, they almost always
are your hard-working, smart people trying to do a good

job, but if their overwhelming mode of operation is, one,
crisis management and, two, avoiding going over budget,

are up to your arse in alligators, it is difficult to drain
the swamps. But the people who know how to drain the

innovation.
Q. So taking that analogy, you are a leading swamp
drainer in the field of peri-operative care --
A. Yes.
Q. -- what is it that you need to do in order to have
that particular change made - that is, to have people
assessed before they go on to the list?
A. One, I think the funding model, if you have an

Q. Let me take it down to a more nuts and bolts level.
You have the expertise and the idea. You have identified
a solution to a problem --
A. Yes.
Q. -- which you say is going to produce better patient

outcomes.
A. Yes.
Q. What do you actually do in terms of - who do you speak
to, or what process do you need to engage in, in order to
bring about that change within your hospital, say?
A. I think there is something to be said for having
a parallel structure, so that while you have got

of getting the work done every day, that there is
a parallel process that is continually and hungrily looking

Q. Dealing with the process that is there at the moment,

A. Well, the surgical services manager, the general
manager, the director of - the DMS.

Q. How would that happen? Would you initiate a meeting
with them or would --
A. Oh, yes, we've talked about it many times.
Q. So you have initiated meetings with those relevant
individuals?
A. Yes.
Q. And discussed what you perceive to be the benefits of
an earlier assessment of someone's appropriateness for the
treatment they are going to receive or need for
pre-habilitation?
A. Yes.
Q. In very rough terms and we don't need the exact date,
when were those meetings or when was that meeting or those
meetings held? Was it very recently or weeks ago, years
ago?
A. Years ago. The current general manager has worked her

A. No.

A. Yes.

A. I think that's what we were doing with that Maggi

THE COMMISSIONER: Q. An alternative could be, for the

A. Yes.

A. But equally, the problem --
Q. I'm thinking of other inquiries broadly there, too.
A. Waiting for people to die is not encouraging.
Q. Sure.
A. But sometimes - and you may remember 10, 15 years ago,

A. I think it should. But it would be - you know,

A. Yes.
